Israel election: Turnout at record levels at halfway stage
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 27, 2026
Almost 45% of the electorate had voted by 2 p.m., the highest share since such records began in 1973. The highly anticipated vote is expected to be a close-fought contest, and perhaps even a stalemate.
What you need to know
- Israelis voting to elect Knesset
- Israel election committee reports highest voter turnout on record as of 2 p.m., halfway through the voting day
- Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, faces a staunch challenge to his grip on power
- His chief rival is former military chief Gadi Eisenkot
- Eisenkot's Yashar party has polled higher than Netanyahu's Likud party
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and its aftermath:
Who are Israel's first-time voters projected to support?
Polls show Israel's many young voters are more likely to vote for far-right parties, particularly Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party.
An opinion poll by Agam Labs at Jerusalem's Hebrew University predicts that supporters of Otzma Yehudit are younger than the average Israeli voter, with as many as a third voting for the first time.
Over 500,000 Israelis have reached voting age since the 2022 election. Of those voters, three in every four define themselves as right or center-right, according to a recent poll for Channel 12. The poll did not survey Palestinian citizens of Israel.
First-time voters were teenagers when Ben-Gvir joined Netanyahu's incumbent government in 2022, making up Israel's most far-right government to date.
A year later, they witnessed the Hamas-led October 7 terror attack which killed 1,200 Israelis, mostly civilians, and saw some 251 others taken hostage and brought to Gaza. The attack triggered a 2-year war on the Palestinian enclave that resulted in tens of thousands of Palestinians killed and intensified settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. Hamas is designated as a terrorist group by several countries.
Previously, Otzma Yehudit's support was concentrated primarily among settlers in the occupied West Bank.
WATCH — Author, politician Avraham Burg on why a Palestinian peace process barely featured in the campaign
While security remained the dominant issue for Israeli voters, one topic was largely absent from the election campaign: a peace process with the Palestinians.
After years of conflict and failed negotiations, that debate has been pushed to the political margins.
Has Israeli society abandoned the idea of coexistence?
Avraham Burg, an Israeli writer and former Speaker of the Israeli Parliament, shares his insights with DW.
Turnout reaches highest level on record at halfway point
Turnout in Israel's election keeps rising. It reached a record 44.9% by 2 p.m. (1200 UTC), the Central Elections Commission said.
Some 3.29 million Israelis had cast their ballots by that point, commission head Dean Livne said.
It was the highest turnout recorded at that hour since the commission began collecting comparable statistics in 1973.
Eisenkot promises 'change' after casting his vote
Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, urged voters on Tuesday to oust what he called the "worst government" in Israel's history and promised a more responsible style of leadership.
"There is a wind of change blowing in Israel, and this change will come into effect tonight at 10 p.m.," at which point polls close, he said after casting his own vote at a polling station in Holon, just south of Tel-Aviv.
"We will not lead Israel through division and scaremongering, but through unity and true love," he said. "We will win!"
Ahead of election day, Israeli pollsters had predicted a close race between Netanyahu's right-wing conservatives and Eisenkot's opposition bloc, with neither expected to win an outright majority.
"I call on all citizens of Israel to vote, not to buckle under the heat or the disruptions, to stick to the mission," said Eisenkot. "To replace tonight the worst government since the state was established."
WATCH: How Israel's PM Netanyahu holds on to power
Three years after the Hamas-led October 7 attacks exposed major flaws in Israeli security, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains the dominant figure in Israel's political landscape. DW examines how many Israeli voters judge him more on his response to the crisis than on the failures that preceded it.
Experts point to security concerns, fear, Israel's conflicts on multiple fronts, and the absence of a clear challenger as key factors behind Netanyahu's resilience. The report also explores why international criticism can strengthen his support ahead of Israel's upcoming Knesset election.
Netanyahu casts ballot, while accusing Arab-Israeli parties of fraud
Israel's Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday that "there are currently no indications of systematic tampering with ballot slips" after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Arab-Israeli parties of "trying to steal the election."
Netanyahu made the allegation after casting his own ballot in Jerusalem while urging voters to choose his Likud party.
"We know what is at stake ... We cannot leave this battle here in the hands of the left and the Arab parties that want to bring an end to the Jewish state," he said.
Netanyahu has used Arab-Israeli parties throughout the election to stoke fears of a Palestinian state and mobilize voters for Likud.
"So no barbecues, don't go to the beach — go to the polling station and vote Likud."
Netanyahu had said that three senior officials from the opposition Ra'am party, which has an Arab Muslim voter base, had been arrested in southern Israel with envelopes full of cash.
The acting director general of the Central Elections Committee, Dean Livne, referred to the "unusual" incident with the envelopes in a press conference Tuesday morning but said that "police, even before people arrived at the polling stations, caught individuals who tried to bribe voters."
He said the unidentified suspects were not actually at polling stations and were caught near their homes, adding the matter was under investigation.
"There are no similar incidents of this kind across the country," he concluded. "This was a localized case."
Opposition parties, including that of Netanyahu's main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, have also complained that ballot papers were being defaced and stolen at polling stations.
Early Israel election turnout highest in decades
Voter turnout in the first three hours of the Israeli general election was the highest in decades, Israel's Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday.
According to the committee, nationwide turnout by mid-morning was already at 16.68%, the highest at this stage of the vote since 1981 and up from 15.9% at the same time in the 2022 election.
"By 10 a.m., more than 1,200,000 Israelis had voted," said the committee's acting director general, Dean Livne.
Total voter turnout in Israeli general elections approached 80% the 1990s but hasn't been higher than 72.3% since the turn of the century. Turnout at the last general election in 2022 was 70.6%.
Turnout among Arab Israelis is expected to be particularly important given the role Arab parties could play as potential kingmakers in coalition talks.
"Our vote will change the government," predicted Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Ra'am party as he cast his vote, adding that he hoped turnout would surpass 70% in Arab communities.
Arabs in Israel make up about 18% of the electorate, and pre-election surveys have suggested a sharp increase in voter participation.
Data from the Midgam Research Institute cited by the Qatar-owned The New Arab indicates that turnout within the Arab community could rise to between 62% and 63%, up from approximately 53% in previous elections. The National, based in the United Arab Emirates, said its sources were predicting an "astronomical" Arab turnout.
How does Israel's election work?
Who is eligible to vote?
Around 7.3 million Israelis (including around 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel) are eligible to vote on Tuesday.
More than 640,000 young Israelis will be eligible to vote in a general election for the first time.
Around 3.1 million Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank do not have the right to vote in Israeli elections, but 500,000 illegal settlers in those territories do.
A further 350,000 Palestinians live in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem and also cannot vote, whereas around 230,000 Israelis living there can.
The US-based non-profit America-Israel Democracy Coalition (AID Coalition) has organized a "Fly&Vote" initiative, with as many as 67,000 voters returning to Israel to participate in the election, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data.
The coalition said half are coming from the US, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Israel does not have postal voting.
How does the voting system work?
Israel is a parliamentary democracy and voters elect a legislature rather than choosing their prime minister directly. Voters choose a party "list."
Israel uses a proportional representation system under which 120 parliamentary seats are distributed roughly in proportion to a party's share of the vote.
To enter parliament (known as the Knesset), parties must receive at least 3.25% of valid votes, which is equivalent to roughly four seats.
The party which can command a majority of at least 61 seats is called upon to form a government. No single party has ever won an outright majority, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions. Polls suggest this year will be no different.
Unlike many other democracies around the world, Israel is not divided up into geographic electoral districts.
Rather than electing individual lawmakers to represent local areas, voters in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem and Haifa all choose from the same party lists in one, single, nationwide constituency.
When polling stations close at 10 p.m. local time (9 p.m. CET), broadcasters will publish their first exit polls, offering an initial indication of the results. Official results are scheduled to be published on November 4.
Arab-Israeli parties: Potential kingmakers in Israel's future ruling coalition?
While the main competition for the largest number of seats is between Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, the Arab parties are projected to play a key role in determining Israel's next ruling coalition.
For a party or coalition to rule, it needs to secure 61 seats in the Knesset.
As per a recent Channel 12 poll, Eisenkot's bloc is hovering around 55 seats, while Netanyahu's bloc is trailing behind with some 51 seats. This means that either bloc would need to form coalitions in order to rule, should the election results come out similar to the polls.
The most likely parties to tip the scales are the Joint List (projected to win around 9 seats) and the Ra'am (projected to win around 5 seats). The Arab minority, who are Palestinian by heritage but Israeli by nationality, make up around a fifth of Israel's eligible voters. Polls suggest a higher turnout rate for the Arab voters than seen in previous elections.
Netanyahu's Likud and Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudi parties attempted last month to ban the Joint List and Ra'am from running in the race, but Israel's Supreme Court reversed the parties' disqualification earlier in October.
Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu have ruled out an alliance with the Arab parties. But analysts suggest such stances are not set in stone and can shift amid coalition talks, a move Netanyahu himself has resorted to in the past.
Gadi Eisenkot: Who is Netanyahu's main opponent?
The Israeli general election is considered by many to be a verdict on the country's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
But who is the opposition, and what do they stand for?
The main opposition force is a so-called "change bloc," a mixed group of center-right and some left-wing parties led by the newly formed Yashar (honesty) party and its leader Gadi Eisenkot.
A relative political newcomer, Eisenkot is the son of Moroccan immigrants who rose to become the chief of the staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) between 2015 and 2019.
Eisenkot has positioned himself squarely in opposition to Netanyahu in terms of his personality — an unpolished man of the people in contrast to the highly stylized and controlling prime minister.
Campaigning on accountability, political reform, and national unity, Eisenkot has sharply criticized Netanyahu's leadership before and after the October 7 Hamas attacks.
But his politics don't differ massively and, although he has emphasized equal rights for all Israeli citizens, he has been ambiguous on the idea of a two-state solution since October 7.
While backing Israel's military operations, he argues the government lacks a clear strategy and has called for an independent inquiry into the failures surrounding the attacks. His military record and the death of his son in the Gaza war have strengthened his standing among many voters
The parties in Eisenkot's bloc all have ideological differences but are united by their goal of removing Netanyahu from power.
Polls open in Israel election
Voting began in Israel at 7 a.m. local time (6 a.m. CET) on Tuesday in the first general election since the deadly Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, and the devastating war in Gaza unleashed by Israel in response.
Some 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote, with polls showing a bloc led by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving premier, neck and neck with Gadi Eisenkot's centrist opposition alliance.
Most polling stations will close at 10 p.m. local time (8 p.m. UTC).
WATCH: Netanyahu's final campaign? — Israel heads to the polls
There's a lot at stake in this election: The fallout and questions of political accountability for the attacks of October 7, 2023; mandatory military service for ultra-Orthodox men and sharing the burden of national defense; along with Israel's standing in the international community.
Nowhere can the division within Israeli society be more felt than in debate over Benjamin Netanyahu.
For the past four years, Israel's long-standing prime minister has led what has been described as the most right-wing government in the country's history. He broke with political convention by forming an alliance with ultranationalist politician Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Many Israelis want to see an end to this government. They blame it for the failures surrounding Hamas' terror attack and for the country's growing isolation internationally. Many are placing their hopes in Gadi Eisenkot, who has emerged as a leading opposition figure to challenge Netanyahu.
Security fears and domestic divides define Israel's election battle
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his top challenger Gadi Eisenkot are both against the creation of an independent Palestinian state, meaning the election is not expected to lead to major policy changes that could revive the long-stalled peace process.
Here are some of the other major campaign issues:
- Security and the War: Voters are focused on the management of the Israel-Hamas war, the future of Gaza, and handling threats from Iran and Hezbollah.
- Military Service: There is an intense debate over whether the exemption for ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) men should be extended or whether they should be required to serve in the military like other Jewish citizens.
- The Justice System: There are deep disagreements over proposed judicial reforms that would change the balance of power between elected politicians and the Supreme Court.
- The Economy: Voters are highly concerned about the cost of living, housing prices, inflation, and war-related spending, although these are not the primary campaign issues.
Welcome to our coverage
Israelis head to the polls today to elect a new Knesset in what is expected to be a tightly contested race.
Incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, is fighting to stay in power, with several court cases awaiting him if he loses office.
Polls suggest his opponent, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is in the lead.
Stay tuned as we closely follow the election, its results and the wider implications for the region.
digest_he:
אחוז ההצבעה בבחירות לכנסת ישראל הגיע לשיא של כל הזמנים באמצע יום הבחירות, כאשר כמעט 45% מהבוחרים מימשו את זכותם עד השעה 14:00, הנתון הגבוה ביותר מאז החלו הרישומים ב-1973. ראש הממשלה בנימין נתניהו מתמודד עם אתגר משמעותי על שלטונו מצד יוכל מפלגת יששר, ראשת האופוזיציה ורמטכ"ל לשעבר גדי איזנקוט, שמפלגתו זכתה בסקרים לתוצאות גבוהות.

במקביל, סקרים מראים כי מצביעים צעירים רבים, שרבים מהם מצביעים לראשונה, נוטים לתמוך במפלגות ימין וימין קיצוני, ובפרט במפלגת עוצמה יהודית בראשותו של איתמר בן גביר. בנוסף, נושא הסכסוך והתהליך המדיני עם הפלסטינים נדחק לשוליים במסע הבחירות, כאשר סוגיות ביטחוניות נותרו במוקד תשומת הלב הציבורית לאחר אירועי 7 באוקטובר.

ביום הבחירות, ראש הממשלה נתניהו האשים את מפלגות ערביות בניסיון להטות את התוצאות, אך ועדת הבחירות המרכזית מסרה כי אין אינדיקציות לזיופים שיטתיים. מנגד, איזנקוט קרא לבוחרים להחליף את הממשלה הנוכחית וטען כי רוח של שינוי מנשבת במדינה לקראת סגירת הקלפיות.
